UNIT 23: AGRICULTURE AND FISHING
Key theme: agriculture and fishing are still significant economic activities in Ireland, but climate change, sustainability and EU policies have changed practices over time.
Learning outcomes 3.1, 3.2, 3.3: examine the importance and changing nature of agriculture in Ireland; explore changes in the Irish fishing industry; discuss the impact of EU policies on agriculture and fisheries.

KEY TERMS - AGRICULTURE
- Agriculture: growing crops and raising animals for food, materials and other products. The world's primary economic activity of food production.
- Cultivation: preparing land and growing crops (planting, watering, caring for plants).
- Output: total amount produced, e.g. how much food a farm produces.
- Yield: amount of crop produced per unit of land, e.g. tonnes of wheat per hectare.
- Commercialised agriculture: all produce is for sale and profit.
- Specialised agriculture: focuses on one main crop or animal, e.g. only dairy or only wheat.
- Organic farming: avoids artificial chemicals (pesticides, fertilisers); uses natural methods.
- Markets: places where farm products are bought and sold.
- Core socio-economic region: well-developed area with a large, wealthy population, strong infrastructure and good access to markets.
- Peripheral socio-economic region: area far from wealthy markets, e.g. the West of Ireland.
- Food processing: changing raw farm products into consumable or longer-lasting forms (milk to cheese, wheat to bread).
- Economically viable: a farm that makes enough profit to sustain the farmer long term.
- Progressive farming: modern methods aiming at efficiency and sustainability. Innovative farming: new ideas, methods or technologies.
- Conservative farming: avoids change, sticks to familiar methods. Traditional farming: long-established methods passed down generations.
- Leaching: nutrients washed down into lower soil horizons.

IMPORTANCE OF AGRICULTURE IN IRELAND
- Traditionally a family-farm model; a big part of Irish identity, economy and society.
- Employs almost 10% of the workforce.
- Agricultural products were 9% of total goods exported in 2024, to over 180 countries; mostly beef and dairy.
- Worth 8% of GDP; a record 17 billion euro in 2024.
- Geofact: Ireland produced 603,000 tonnes of beef in 2024, 90% exported - enough to feed 8.2 million people 200 g of beef a day for a year.

TYPES OF FARMING
- Pastoral: raising animals (cattle, sheep, pigs, goats).
- Arable/tillage: growing cereals (wheat, barley, oats) or vegetables (potatoes, carrots, onions, cabbage).
- Dairying: producing milk from cows.
- Mixed: animals and crops on one farm.
- Horticulture/market gardening: fresh fruit, salad crops and vegetables in a confined space (a few hectares, a garden or greenhouse); sometimes called urban farming.
- Organic: no artificial fertilisers or pesticides.
- Commercial: all produce sold for profit; run like a business.
- Subsistence: much produce eaten by the farm family, or too little to profit.
- Extensive (expansive): large area, less labour, e.g. grazing animals.
- Intensive: land continuously cultivated; limited space, urban areas, commercial farming.

FACTORS AFFECTING AGRICULTURE: ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIO-ECONOMIC, POLITICAL
CLIMATE
- Cool temperate oceanic climate suits many farming types.
- West: about 1,600 mm rain a year (relief rainfall, near the Atlantic) - almost twice the East and Southeast (about 800 mm), which are in the rain shadow of the western mountains.
- Relief rain diagram in words: warm moist air rises over high ground, cools and condenses into clouds and rain on the windward side; air descends on the far side, warms and becomes drier - the rain shadow.
- Winters mild, 5-6 degrees C; summers 15-16 degrees C.
- West and South: wetter, suits grass and pastoral farming; limits cereals due to leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease. Very high rainfall formed infertile blanket bogs on mountains.
- East and Southeast: less leaching, drier, more crops; less cloud gives a growing season of 280 days - over a month longer than the western seaboard.
- Climate change: more vector-borne diseases like bluetongue; ticks and mosquitoes active longer; more crop fungal diseases and pests; flooding and storms damage infrastructure, livestock, soil and crops; pollinators such as honeybees threatened. But a longer growing season may boost grass yields (beef and dairy) and allow earlier harvests. Farmers must adapt.
RELIEF AND DRAINAGE
- Relief: steepness of the land. Drainage: movement of excess water through the landscape.
- West: Caledonian fold mountains - Blue Stack Mountains (Donegal), Ox Mountains (Sligo), Nephin Beg Range (Mayo), Maamturk Mountains and Twelve Pins (Galway). Steep slopes make machinery and transport networks difficult (e.g. around Croagh Patrick).
- Severe glacial erosion in the last Ice Age stripped soil, leaving rocky infertile uplands; high rainfall and poor drainage cause waterlogging.
- Result: western farms average 25.5 hectares vs national average 32.5 hectares. Over 20% of Ireland's grassland is in the Western Region - less profitable sheep and dry stock cattle (fattened for beef). Less than 2% of Irish cereal was grown in the West in 2023.
- East: undulating, well-drained lowland (except Dublin-Wicklow Mountains), rarely floods; easy to use machinery; warmer for longer so longer growing season; easier to build transport networks. Average farm 42 hectares; more commercialised and specialised.
SOILS
- West: mostly infertile. Peat soils (acidic, poor minerals, waterlogged) on uplands of west Donegal, west Mayo, west Galway. Granite in west Galway weathers to poor clay soils unsuitable for tillage.
- East Mayo: podzols - severely leached; hard pans around Ballyhaunis cause poor drainage and waterlogging; low tillage yields.
- Brown earths in east Galway, south Roscommon and central Mayo support some dairying, but they are shallow and heavy rain limits yields.
- East and South: deep, fertile brown earths, rich in nutrients and humus; do not waterlog in wet spells or dry out in dry spells; little leaching; well-drained.
SOCIO-ECONOMIC FACTORS
- Markets: large, urban, wealthy populations support large commercial specialist farms. The Greater Dublin Area is a core region - a market of over 2 million people.
- Food processing in the Greater Dublin Area: wheat and barley farmers supply the Guinness brewery in Dublin; Tayto Snacks, Ashbourne, Co. Meath sources potatoes from Meath, Dublin, Wexford and Louth; Green Isle, Co. Kildare uses local vegetables for frozen food; beef to local processing plants; horticulture in north Co. Dublin, Wicklow and Wexford supplies supermarkets and markets daily (e.g. Moore Street market).
- Excellent transport gets perishable produce to market fast, lowering costs; Dublin Port and Airport reach EU and British markets.
- West: lower density population, limited local market, far from Dublin, Britain and the EU - higher transport costs, commercial farming less viable (peripheral region). Galway City is a market and the M6 improved links, but most of the West has a poor, underfunded transport network.
- Over half of western farmers are part-time with another job. Teagasc (national agriculture and food development authority): almost two-thirds of western farms are not economically viable.
- Commercialisation, age and gender: East and South farmers are younger, more progressive, use technology and innovation - more efficient and profitable. Larger farms in the Greater Dublin Area and the Golden Vale of Munster; the larger the farm, the younger the farmer is likely to be.
- West: less commercialised, older farmers, more conservative and traditional, smaller farms, not intensively farmed; older farmers favour less labour-intensive sheep farming; less appealing for young people to take over; some farms abandoned; move away from father-to-son inheritance.
- CSO Farm Structure Survey 2023: the West has the highest share of female farmers (13.9%); Mayo highest by county (15%); Monaghan has the highest share of male farmers (89.9%).

POLITICAL FACTORS: THE COMMON AGRICULTURAL POLICY (CAP)
- After World War II there were food shortages in Europe. In 1962 the EEC introduced the CAP to: increase food production (stable, safe food supply) and modernise agriculture.
- Ireland joined the EEC in 1973 and implemented the CAP immediately. Irish farming shifted from small subsistence family farms to a specialised, market-centred, environmentally conscious industry.
PHASE 1: PRODUCTION AND MODERNISATION (1970s-1990s)
- Intervention and subsidies: guaranteed minimum prices for milk, beef, cereals. A Guarantee Fund bought any surplus once it reached this minimum price.
- Market protection: no tariffs or import duties on farm produce within the EEC, so EEC produce was cheaper than outside imports.
- Headage Payment Scheme (1975): payment per animal for pastoral and dairy farmers - big rise in sheep and cattle numbers and milk production.
- Grants for modernisation; rapid growth in output and incomes; farmers specialised in dairy and beef; fewer, larger farms; traditional mixed farms replaced by specialised, export-focused farms.
PHASE 2: CAP REFORMS, DECOUPLING AND DIRECT INCOME SUPPORTS (1984-2015)
- Problem: overproduction caused by the Guarantee Fund; rising costs of storing surpluses; EU food prices among the highest in the world.
- Milk quotas (1984): limit on milk a farmer was paid for, based on 1983 output; fines for extra milk. Many switched to dry stock (beef) or sheep; others bought extra quota.
- Milk quotas abolished in 2015 after a CAP 'health check' found growing global dairy demand. Over 18,000 farmers spent over 1.4 billion euro expanding herds; Irish dairying became the fastest-growing dairy market in the EU; more milk to processors Tirlan, Dairygold and Kerry Group. Dairy farms: 80,000 (1984), 17,500 (2014), 15,319 (2024); output per farm 70,000 litres (1984), 300,000 (2014), 585,000 (2024). Dairy incomes have risen since abolition.
- MacSharry Reforms (1992, named after Irish EU Commissioner Ray MacSharry): shifted from price support to income support; cereal intervention prices cut by 30%, smaller cuts for beef and butter; set-aside paid cereal farmers for every hectare they did not farm.
- Rural Environment Protection Scheme (REPS, 1994): farmers as custodians of the land; paid from the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) for replanting native hedges and trees, not cutting hedgerows in nesting season, reducing chemical runoff, preventing overgrazing of hillsides, maintaining drystone walls.
- Decoupling (2003, Fischler Reforms, after Austrian Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler): removed payments tied to production (like headage); income support based on farm size not herd size; farmers produce for the open market. Single Farm Payment (SFP) fully separated payments from production. Stable income without pressure to intensify. 'Front-loading' redistributed payments from larger to small and medium farms - a safety net for small and part-time farmers. Funding shifted towards rural development and environment; aim: more competitive, sustainable, less dependent agriculture.
- Sugar reforms: early 2000s, Brazil and other non-EU countries protested to the World Trade Organization (WTO) about unfair EU sugar support. In 2006 the EU cut the guaranteed sugar price by 36% and reduced quotas over four years. Cheap imports from the Caribbean and South and Central America flooded in; over 3,700 Irish sugar beet farmers affected; processing plants in Carlow (opened 1926, Ireland's first) and Mallow closed. This destroyed the Irish sugar industry.
PHASE 3: GREEN TRANSITION (2010s-present)
- Focus on climate change and biodiversity loss.
- REPS replaced by GLAS (Green Low-Carbon Agri-Environment Scheme) in 2014 - protect water quality and endangered flora and fauna. Replaced in 2023 by ACRES (Agri-Climate Rural Environment Scheme) - improve biodiversity, climate, air and water quality.
- CAP Strategic Plan 2021-2027 has strong environmental goals (ten CAP objectives include fair income, competitiveness, food value chain, climate change, environmental care, landscapes, generational renewal, rural areas, food and health, innovation).
- TAMS (Targeted Agriculture Modernisation Schemes): grants to adopt sustainable practices - soil health, biodiversity, lower emissions; also grants to increase farm size, build new buildings and upgrade technology.
IMPACTS OF CAP ON RURAL DEVELOPMENT AND FOOD SAFETY
- Early Retirement from Farming Scheme (ERS): pensions for farmers over 55 to retire and rent or sell land to younger farmers; ended 2006. A new collaborative farming grant encourages older-younger partnerships.
- Disadvantaged Area Grants for areas with poor soil, mountains or poor drainage; replaced by the LEADER programme.
- Agri-Tourism Scheme via the Rural Innovation and Development Fund (RIDF), 300,000 euro for projects: grants for green energy, organic products, open farms, farmhouse B&Bs, country walks - alternative incomes.
- Food quality, safety, animal welfare: traceability introduced in 2002; Farm-to-Fork strategy (2020) lets consumers trace beef and lamb back to the farm - better quality, more confidence, higher demand and profits.

CHANGING AGRICULTURAL PRACTICES
- Move away from intensive farming: intensive dairy and beef increase greenhouse gases - methane from livestock and nitrous oxide from nitrogen fertilisers; nutrient runoff (nitrates, phosphates) from slurry and fertilisers pollutes streams, rivers and lakes.
- Food Vision 2030: aims to make Ireland a global leader in sustainable food systems. Practices: rewetting land to trap carbon; reducing herd sizes; planting legumes (peas, beans) that do not need fertiliser; cover crops such as brassicas that trap nutrients; better soil pH and nutrient levels.
- Organic farming: organically farmed area tripled 2020-2026; over 4,000 organic farms by 2026. Driven by consumer demand for chemical-free food and understanding of healthy soil. Uses crop rotation, integrated pest management (IPM, e.g. ladybirds as natural enemies) and natural fertilisers.
- IPM: combines cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical methods with monitoring and pest identification; avoids excessive pesticide use, conserves biodiversity, protects food security.
- Urban food production: community gardens and allotments; vertical farming and hydroponics (plants grown in water-based minerals rather than soil) - year-round, controlled, minimal space, 90% less water. Emerald Greens (2021) was Ireland's first commercial vertical farm, supplying local pesticide-free food. Reduces food miles and waste.
- Technology: drones, satellite imagery, farm management software, automated milking. Precision agriculture uses sensors and GPS to apply fertiliser and water exactly, reducing waste; farmers monitor grass growth by phone. Agri-Tech robotics raises profits and labour efficiency and helps meet climate targets. Dairy robots can milk cows, record yields and check cow health.

THE IRISH FISHING INDUSTRY
- Smaller than agriculture but important for coastal communities. About 8,000 directly employed (2026); worth 1.24 billion euro. Relatively low given warm, unpolluted waters and a long continental shelf rich in plankton.
- Ireland's maritime territory: 880,000 km2, over ten times its land area - bigger than France's land area (632,702 km2).
KEY TERMS - FISHING
- Continental shelf: shallow seabed around a coast before deep ocean. Plankton: tiny drifting organisms at the base of the marine food chain.
- Aquaculture: farming fish or shellfish in controlled water environments.
- Maritime territories: sea areas a country controls. Landing: bringing caught fish ashore. Fisher: person who catches fish for a job.
- Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM): state agency supporting fishing and seafood. Sea-Fisheries Protection Authority (SFPA): enforces fishing laws.
- Sustainable fishing: not harming fish populations or the environment.
- Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY): largest catch possible without reducing future stocks.
- Landing obligation: fishers must bring all catches ashore, even unwanted ones.
- Relative Stability Principle (RSP): each EU country gets a fixed share of quotas.
- Angling: fishing with rod and line, usually for sport.
TYPES OF FISHERIES
- Demersal: live on the seafloor - cod, haddock, plaice.
- Pelagic: live and feed in open water - mackerel, herring.
- Shellfish: invertebrates - crustaceans (hard jointed shell: lobsters, crabs, shrimps, prawns) and molluscs (shell with soft interior: clams).
- Over 50 years Irish fishing changed from small boats to a modern, high-tech industry, mainly after joining the EEC (1973) and the Common Fisheries Policy; growing focus on sustainability and aquaculture.
IMPACT OF EEC/EU MEMBERSHIP
- Ireland gave up control of its maritime territory and shared its waters. Foreign trawlers with modern technology overfished; herring and cod almost wiped out in the late 1970s. CSO: 36% of fish landings in Ireland in 2024 were by foreign trawlers.
- Free access to the world's largest fish import market: in 2024, 55.9% of Irish seafood sold to EU states, worth 385 million euro.
COMMON FISHERIES POLICY (CFP) AND EMFAF
- CFP introduced 1983 to manage fish stocks for all members and promote a sustainable, viable industry. In 2021 upgraded with the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund (EMFAF), running to 2027.
- Key measures: Total Allowable Catch (TAC) quotas per state per season; embargoes (total bans) on endangered species; limited seasons and days at sea; minimum mesh size increased to 100 mm so young fish escape; Irish Conservation Box (1986), a 100,000 km2 zone (reduced 2003) protecting spawning grounds of cod, herring and whiting, where only Irish vessels fish with restricted access; exclusion zones around the coast for foreign fleets (the chapter gives 22 km2 for all foreign fleets and 370 km2 for non-European fleets); Maximum Sustainable Yield (2014), calculated by marine biologists; landing obligation (2019) banning wasteful discarding - full catch counted against quota.
- Challenges: Ireland has about 12% of EU fishing waters but a small share of the catch - as little as 15% of the catch value from Irish waters. The RSP locked quotas to early-1980s catches - seen as unfair; large Spanish and French fleets exploit Irish waters. After Brexit (2020) Irish quota value fell by 50 million euro a year and the season was halved.
- Decommissioning: 1980s quota system and boat reduction schemes; fishers retired via the Retirement Pension Scheme and decommissioned trawlers - job losses, especially on the Western Seaboard. Rising fish prices from high demand and lower supply; employment, catches and incomes fell in many communities.
- Benefits: access to the EU single market (450 million consumers); funding to modernise fleets, infrastructure and processing; until 2013 grants to replace old boats with high-tech trawlers. Catches and exports rose from 2.7 million Irish pounds (1970) to 1.24 billion euro (2024). Labelling and traceability raise confidence.
- EU funds provided SFPA vessels (part of the naval service) - less illegal fishing; SFPA can inspect, seize, detain and prosecute (e.g. undersized fish); fines and confiscation.
- TACs and MSY prevented collapse of many species; landing obligation encourages selective fishing. 2013 reforms withdrew fleet-upgrade grants, aiming to reduce fleet sizes. Since 2021 scientific data collection on stock health. EMFAF modernised harbours, freezer and processing plants at Killybegs, Co. Donegal (largest fishing port) and Baltimore, Co. Cork; supports aquaculture. Other ports include Castletownbere, Howth, Dingle, Rossaveal, Greencastle, Kinsale.
AQUACULTURE
- Grew as wild stocks came under pressure. Freshwater trout existed mid-20th century; industry took off in the 1970s-80s, focusing on Atlantic salmon, mussels and oysters. Example: Clare Island salmon farmed in Clew Bay, Co. Mayo; also Ballinakill Bay, Connemara.
- Ideal conditions: indented coastline, sheltered bays, clean unpolluted water. BIM and Udaras na Gaeltachta gave financial and technical support; licensing regulates it.
- Ireland is a world leader in organically certified farmed fish.
- Challenges: disease, sea lice, escaped farmed fish cross-breeding with wild fish; strict guidelines now.
- 2024: 1,908 directly employed; worth 211 million euro, up almost 30 million on the previous year.
- Clew Bay: mussels, oysters, scallops, abalone, salmon, sea trout; over 100 employed; supports 'gastronomic tourism' on the Wild Atlantic Way (Westport).
INLAND FISHERIES
- Freshwater fisheries (salmon, trout) threatened by pollution (fertiliser runoff) and overfishing.
- Inland Fisheries Ireland (IFI, 2010) conserves, protects and manages inland fisheries and sea angling. Inland Fisheries Act 2010 and Fisheries (Consolidation) Act 1959: catch limits and seasons, bans on nets, traps, spears and barbed 'poacher' hooks, protecting spawning habitats. IFI combats illegal fishing and invasive species and funds community conservation. Protects wild salmon and brown trout - natural heritage and a draw for anglers and tourists.

rows.prompt: Roughly what share of the Irish workforce does agriculture employ?

Farming where most produce is eaten by the farm family

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between commercial and subsistence farming.
rows.model_answer: Commercial farming sells all its produce for profit and the farm is run like a business. In subsistence farming much of the produce is eaten by the farmer and family, or production is too low to make a profit.

rows.prompt: Describe in words a diagram explaining relief rainfall and the rain shadow in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Warm, moist air from the Atlantic rises over the western mountains, cools and condenses to form clouds and rain on the western side. The air then descends on the eastern side, warms and becomes drier, so the East lies in a rain shadow and gets about 800 mm compared with 1,600 mm in the West.

rows.prompt: Explain how soils differ between the West and the East of Ireland.
rows.model_answer: The West has mostly infertile soils: acidic, waterlogged peat on uplands, leached podzols with hard pans in east Mayo, and poor clay from granite in west Galway. The East and South have deep, fertile brown earths rich in nutrients and humus that are well-drained and suffer little leaching, suiting many crops.

rows.prompt: Explain how the age profile of farmers affects farming in the West of Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Western farmers tend to be older than average with conservative, traditional attitudes. They often choose less labour-intensive, less profitable sheep farming, and farming is less attractive for young family members to take over, so some farms are abandoned.

rows.prompt: Explain why reforms were made to the CAP from 1984 onwards.
rows.model_answer: The Guarantee Fund bought any surplus at a guaranteed price, causing overproduction. EU countries were unhappy with the rising cost of funding surplus produce, especially as European food prices were among the highest in the world. Reforms such as milk quotas, MacSharry's price cuts and decoupling were introduced to control this.

rows.prompt: Name three sustainable farming practices now being used in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: Rewetting land to trap carbon; reducing herd sizes to lower methane; planting legume crops such as peas and beans that do not need fertiliser; planting cover crops like brassicas to trap nutrients; and organic methods such as crop rotation and integrated pest management.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between demersal and pelagic fish, giving an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Demersal fish live on or near the seafloor, such as cod, haddock and plaice. Pelagic fish live and feed in open water away from the bottom and shore, such as mackerel and herring.

rows.prompt: What is aquaculture and why has it grown in Ireland?
rows.model_answer: Aquaculture is the farming of fish or shellfish in controlled water environments. It grew as wild stocks came under pressure, and Ireland's indented coastline, sheltered bays and clean water are ideal, with support from BIM and Udaras na Gaeltachta. In 2024 it employed 1,908 people and was worth 211 million euro.

rows.prompt: Describe and explain the impact of European Union (EU) policies on agriculture in Ireland. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) was introduced in 1962 to increase food production and modernise farming. When Ireland joined the EEC in 1973 farmers got guaranteed minimum prices for milk, beef and cereals, with a Guarantee Fund buying surpluses. Market protection meant no tariffs within the EEC. The 1975 Headage Payment Scheme paid per animal, causing a dramatic rise in sheep, cattle and milk. Grants encouraged modernisation, so farms became fewer, larger and specialised in dairy and beef. However, overproduction became costly, so milk quotas were introduced in 1984, based on 1983 output; many farmers switched to beef or sheep. In 1992 the MacSharry Reforms cut cereal prices by 30% and introduced set-aside. REPS (1994) paid farmers to protect hedgerows and drystone walls. In 2003 decoupling based payments on farm size, through the Single Farm Payment, giving stable incomes. The 2006 sugar reforms cut prices by 36%, closing plants in Carlow and Mallow and affecting 3,700 farmers. Quotas were abolished in 2015, and dairying became the EU's fastest-growing. Today GLAS, ACRES and TAMS support a green transition.
rows.marking_scheme: 15 SRPs x 2m = 30m. Credit: CAP aims/1962; 1973 entry; intervention/guaranteed prices; Guarantee Fund; market protection; Headage 1975; modernisation/fewer larger farms; overproduction; milk quotas 1984; MacSharry 1992/30%/set-aside; REPS 1994; decoupling 2003/SFP; front-loading; sugar 2006/Carlow/Mallow; quota abolition 2015 and dairy growth; GLAS/ACRES/TAMS; ERS; Farm-to-Fork traceability. Max 6 SRPs if only one phase discussed.

rows.prompt: Examine how physical factors influence agriculture in the West of Ireland compared with the East. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: Climate differs between West and East. The West receives about 1,600 mm of relief rainfall a year, almost twice the 800 mm of the East, which lies in the rain shadow. High rainfall suits grass and pastoral farming but limits cereals through leaching, waterlogging and fungal disease, and has formed infertile blanket bog. The East's drier, sunnier weather gives a 280-day growing season, over a month longer than the West, favouring tillage. Relief also matters. The West is dominated by Caledonian fold mountains such as the Twelve Pins and Nephin Beg Range, whose steep slopes hinder machinery and transport. Glaciers stripped soil from uplands, and poor drainage causes waterlogging. So western farms average 25.5 hectares, mainly sheep and dry stock, with less than 2% of cereals grown there in 2023. The East is undulating, well-drained lowland where machinery can work large fields, and farms average 42 hectares. Soils complete the contrast: the West has acidic, waterlogged peat in west Mayo and Galway, leached podzols with hard pans around Ballyhaunis, and poor clay from granite. The East and South have deep, fertile brown earths rich in humus that drain well and support crops from wheat to potatoes.

rows.prompt: In relation to a named EU policy, explain one positive impact and one negative impact of that policy on fisheries in Ireland. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Positive: under the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), Irish fishers have free access to the EU single market of 450 million consumers; in 2024 55.9% of Irish seafood went to EU states. EU grants modernised the fleet with high-tech trawlers and funded harbours and processing plants at Killybegs and Baltimore. Exports rose from 2.7 million Irish pounds in 1970 to 1.24 billion euro in 2024. Negative: Ireland had to share its waters. Although it has 12% of EU waters, Irish fishers may get as little as 15% of the catch value, as the Relative Stability Principle locked in early-1980s quotas. Larger Spanish and French trawlers fish close to our coast. After Brexit, Irish quota value fell by 50 million euro a year and the season was halved.
rows.marking_scheme: Named policy 2m. Positive impact: 4 SRPs x 2m = 8m. Negative impact: 5 SRPs x 2m = 10m. rows.prompt: Describe how the development of aquaculture has led to change in the fishing industry in Ireland. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: As wild fish stocks came under pressure, the industry turned to fish farming. Freshwater trout farming existed in the mid-20th century, but aquaculture took off in the 1970s and 1980s, shifting to marine farming of Atlantic salmon, mussels and oysters. Ireland's indented coastline, sheltered bays and clean, unpolluted water are ideal. BIM and Udaras na Gaeltachta gave financial and technical support, and licensing regulates the sector. Clare Island salmon is farmed in Clew Bay, Co. Mayo, where over 100 people work and seafood supports gastronomic tourism around Westport. Ireland is now a world leader in organically certified farmed fish. In 2024, 1,908 people were directly employed and the sector was worth 211 million euro. Challenges include disease, sea lice and escaped fish breeding with wild fish.
rows.marking_scheme: 10 SRPs x 2m = 20m. Credit: reason (pressure on wild stocks); timeline; species; physical advantages; BIM/Udaras support; licensing; named example (Clew Bay/Clare Island, Ballinakill Bay); organic leadership; employment and value statistics; challenges and regulation; tourism link.
